1.o: Israel was now to be formed into a commonwealth, or rather a kingdom; for "the Lord was their King" (1 Sam. xii. 12), their government a theocracy, and Moses under him was king in Jeshurun, Deut. xxxiii. 5. Now, for the right settlement of this holy state, next to the institution of good laws was necessary the institution of good order; and account therefore must be taken of the subjects of this kingdom, which is done in this chapter, where we have, I. Orders given to Moses to number the people, ver. 1-4. II.
1.i: Numbers begins with a count and a map: who was in the camp, and where every tribe was to stand around the tent.
1.p: Lord, You know every one of Your people by name. Thank You for counting us as Yours, and for living in our midst. Amen.
1.l: Count something good today, like blessings or friends, and thank God for each one.
q: Some are multiplied greatly and then diminished. What season of growth or shrinking are you in, and who is counting with you?

2.o: The thousands of Israel, having been mustered in the former chapter, in this are marshalled, and a regular disposition is made of their camp, by a divine appointment. Here is, I. A general order concerning it, ver. 1, 2. II. Particular directions for the posting of each of the tribes, in four distinct squadrons, three tribes in each squadron. 1. In the van-guard on the east were posted Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun, ver. 3-9. 2. In the right wing, southward, Reuben, Simeon, and Gad, ver. 10-16. 3.
2.i: Numbers begins with a count and a map: who was in the camp, and where every tribe was to stand around the tent.
2.p: Lord, You know every one of Your people by name. Thank You for counting us as Yours, and for living in our midst. Amen.
2.l: Count something good today, like blessings or friends, and thank God for each one.
q: Some are multiplied greatly and then diminished. What season of growth or shrinking are you in, and who is counting with you?

3.o: This chapter and the next are concerning the tribe of Levi, which was to be mustered and marshalled by itself, and not in common with the other tribes, intimating the particular honour put upon them and the particular duty and service required from them. The Levites are in this chapter considered, I. As attendants on, and assistants to, the priests in the temple-service. And so we have an account, 1. Of the priests themselves (ver. 1-4) and their work, ver. 10. 2. Of the gift of the Levites to them (ver.
3.i: Numbers 3 and 4 assign each family of the tribe of Levi to its own load, and show how carefully the holy things were handled on the road.
3.p: Lord, You give each of us a load to carry in Your house. Make us faithful in our part, however small it seems. Amen.
3.l: Thank someone today who does a hard job that no one sees.
q: Some would think it a disparagement to have their eldest sons serve. What do you hold back from serving because it seems beneath you?

4.o: In the former chapter an account was taken of the whole tribe of Levi, in this we have an account of those of that tribe who were in the prime of their time for service, betwixt thirty and fifty years old. I. The serviceable men of the Kohathites are ordered to be numbered, and their charges are given them, ver. 2-20. II. Of the Gershonites, ver. 24-28. III. Of the Merarites, ver. 29-33. IV. The numbers of each, and the sum total at last, are recorded, ver. 34, &c.
4.i: Numbers 3 and 4 assign each family of the tribe of Levi to its own load, and show how carefully the holy things were handled on the road.
4.p: Lord, You give each of us a load to carry in Your house. Make us faithful in our part, however small it seems. Amen.
4.l: Thank someone today who does a hard job that no one sees.
q: Some would think it a disparagement to have their eldest sons serve. What do you hold back from serving because it seems beneath you?

5.o: In this chapter we have, I. An order, pursuant to the laws already made, for the removing of the unclean out of the camp, ver. 1-4. II. A repetition of the laws concerning restitution, in case of wrong done to a neighbour (ver. 5-8), and concerning the appropriating of the hallowed things to the priests, ver. 9, 10. III. A new law made concerning the trial of a wife suspected of adultery, by the waters of jealousy, ver. 11, &c.
5.i: Numbers 5 keeps the camp clean, insists that wrongs be repaid with interest, and describes an unusual test for a suspicious husband.
5.p: Lord, You live in the middle of Your people. Keep us clean, and make us quick to put our wrongs right. Amen.
5.l: Think of something you have borrowed or broken, and give it back or fix it today.
q: Confession, repayment and a fifth more is a high standard. What would it take for you to meet it?

6.o: In this chapter we have, I. The law concerning Nazarites, 1. What it was to which the vow of a Nazarite obliged him, ver. 1-8. 2. A remedial law in case a Nazarite happened to be polluted by the touch of a dead body, ver. 9-12. 3. The solemnity of his discharge when his time was up, ver. 13-21. II. Instructions given to the priests how they should bless the people, ver. 22, &c.
6.i: Numbers 6 pairs a promise to set oneself apart with the oldest and best-known blessing in the Bible.
6.p: The Lord bless us and keep us; the Lord make His face shine on us and be gracious to us; the Lord give us His peace. Amen.
6.l: Say the Lord bless you to someone today, and mean it.
q: God put the very words of blessing in the priests' mouths. Who needs to hear a blessing from you in plain words?

7.o: God having set up house (as it were) in the midst of the camp of Israel, the princes of Israel here come a visiting with their presents, as tenants to their landlord, in the name of their respective tribes. I. They brought presents, 1. Upon the dedication of the tabernacle, for the service of that, ver. 1-9. 2. Upon the dedication of the altar, for the use of that, ver. 10-88. And, II. God graciously signified his acceptance of them, ver. 89.
7.i: Numbers 7 is the second-longest chapter in the Bible by verse count, and it is one gift described twelve times.
7.p: Lord, You see every gift, large and small. Teach us to give cheerfully, and to honor what others bring. Amen.
7.l: Notice what someone else is giving, and thank them for it, even if their gift looks like yours.
q: The Kohathites had no wagons, because the holiest things were carried on shoulders. What do you carry by hand because it matters too much to wheel?

8.o: This chapter is concerning the lamps or lights of the sanctuary. I. The burning lamps in the candlestick, which the priests were charged to tend, ver. 1-4. II. The living lamps (if I may so call them), The Levites, who as ministers were burning and shining lights. The ordination of the priests we had an account of, Lev. viii. Here we have an account of the ordination of the Levites, the inferior clergy. 1. How they were purified, ver. 5-8. 2. How they were parted with by the people, ver. 9, 10. 3.
8.s: Lighting the Lamps, Cleansing the Levites
8.i: Numbers 8 shows the lampstand being lit and the Levites being cleansed and presented to the Lord for their work.
8.p: Lord, You set people apart to serve in Your house. Light our way, and make us faithful servants. Amen.
8.l: Do a job today that helps others see better, like turning on a light or tidying a dim corner.
q: The elders stood in for the whole people. Who stands in for you in prayer, and for whom do you?

9.o: This chapter is, I. Concerning the great ordinance of the passover; 1. Orders given for the observance of it, at the return of the year, ver. 1-5. 2. Provisos added in regard to such as should be ceremonially unclean, or otherwise disabled, at the time when the passover was to be kept, ver. 6-14. II. Concerning the great favour of the pillar of cloud, which was a guide to Israel through the wilderness, ver. 15, &c.
9.s: The Cloud and the Silver Trumpets
9.i: Numbers 9 and 10 close the time at Sinai: a second chance at the Passover, a cloud that decided every move, and two silver trumpets.
9.p: Lord, lead us as You led Israel, by day and by night, and give us the patience to follow when we cannot see far ahead. Amen.
9.l: Ask God this morning where He wants you to go today, and then go where the day leads.
q: There is no time lost while we are waiting God's time. What are you waiting on that feels like lost time?

10.o: In this chapter we have, I. Orders given about the making and using of silver trumpets, which seems to have been the last of all the commandments God gave upon Mount Sinai, and one of the least, yet not without its significancy, ver. 1-10. II. The history of the removal of Israel's camp from Mount Sinai, and their orderly march into the wilderness of Paran, ver. 11-28. III. Moses's treaty with Hobab, his brother-in-law, ver. 29-32. IV. Moses's prayer at the removing and resting of the ark, ver. 33, &c.
10.s: The Cloud and the Silver Trumpets
10.i: Numbers 9 and 10 close the time at Sinai: a second chance at the Passover, a cloud that decided every move, and two silver trumpets.
10.p: Lord, lead us as You led Israel, by day and by night, and give us the patience to follow when we cannot see far ahead. Amen.
10.l: Ask God this morning where He wants you to go today, and then go where the day leads.
q: There is no time lost while we are waiting God's time. What are you waiting on that feels like lost time?

11.o: Hitherto things had gone pretty well in Israel; little interruption had been given to the methods of God's favour to them since the matter of the golden calf; the people seemed teachable in marshalling and purifying the camp, the princes devout and generous in dedicating the altar, and there was good hope that they would be in Canaan presently.
11.i: The Israelites tire of manna and long for Egypt's food, forgetting their slavery.
11.p: Lord, forgive our complaining. Make us thankful for what You give, every day. Amen.
11.l: Say thank you for your meal today, even if it isn't your favorite.
q: The Israelites were tired of what God gave them each day. What do you take for granted?

12.o: In the foregoing chapter we had the vexation which the people gave to Moses; in this we have his patience tried by his own relations. I. Miriam and Aaron, his own brother and sister, affronted him, ver. 1-3. II. God called them to an account for it, ver. 4-9. III. Miriam was smitten with a leprosy for it, ver. 10. IV. Aaron submits, and Moses meekly intercedes for Miriam, ver. 11-13. V. She is healed, but put to shame for seven days, ver. 14-16.
12.i: Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses, God defends him, and Miriam is struck with disease until Moses prays for her.
12.p: Lord, keep us from jealousy. Make us humble like Moses, and teach us to pray for those who criticize us. Amen.
12.l: If you feel jealous of someone, say a prayer for them instead of saying something unkind.
q: Moses did not defend himself but prayed for the one who hurt him. How do you answer criticism?

13.o: It is a memorable and very melancholy story which is related in this and the following chapter, of the turning back of Israel from the borders of Canaan, when they were just ready to set foot in it, and the sentencing of them to wander and perish in the wilderness for their unbelief and murmuring. It is referred to Ps. xcv. 7, &c., and improved for warning to Christians, Heb. iii. 7, &c. In this chapter we have, I. The sending of twelve spies before them into Canaan, ver. 1-16. II.
13.i: Moses sends twelve spies to explore Canaan, and they return after forty days with a giant cluster of grapes.
13.p: Lord, You give good gifts. Give us courage to look at what You have promised. Amen.
13.l: Try a new fruit today, and imagine what it would be like to find that fruit growing in a new land.
q: The spies saw the same land and came back with different reports. What do you see when you look at a hard thing?

14.o: This chapter gives us an account of that fatal quarrel between God and Israel upon which, for their murmuring and unbelief, he swore in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest. Here is, I. The mutiny and rebellion of Israel against God, upon the report of the evil spies, ver. 1-4. II. The fruitless endeavour of Moses and Aaron, Caleb and Joshua, to still the tumult, ver. 5-10. III. Their utter ruin justly threatened by an offended God, ver. 11, 12. IV. The humble intercession of Moses for them, ver.
14.i: Ten explorers frighten Israel, but Joshua and Caleb urge them to trust God, and Israel is sentenced to forty years in the wilderness.
14.p: Lord, give us a different spirit, one that trusts You when others are afraid. Amen.
14.l: Stand up for what is right today, even if you are the only one.
q: Joshua and Caleb saw the same land as the other ten, but trusted God. What do you see differently when you trust Him?

15.o: This chapter, which is mostly concerning sacrifice and offering, comes in between the story of two rebellions (one ch. xiv. the other ch. xvi.), to signify that these legal institutions were typical of the gifts which Christ was to receive even for the rebellious, Ps. lxviii. 18. In the foregoing chapter, upon Israel's provocation, God had determined to destroy them, and in token of his wrath had sentenced them to perish in the wilderness. But, upon Moses' intercession, he said, "I have pardoned;"
15.i: Numbers 15 comes right after Israel's worst failure, and starts with a promise: when you enter the land.
15.p: Lord, help us remember Your commands and Your goodness every time we look down at our own two hands. Amen.
15.l: Pick something small you can see every day, and let it remind you to pray.
q: The first of the dough was to be given first. What do you give first, before you've counted what is left?

16.o: The date of the history contained in this chapter is altogether uncertain. Probably these mutinies happened after their removal back again from Kadesh-barnea, when they were fixed (if I may so speak) for their wandering in the wilderness, and began to look upon that as their settlement. Presently after new laws given follows the story of a new rebellion, as if sin took occasion from the commandment to become more exceedingly sinful. Here is, I.
16.i: Numbers 16 tells how a Levite and a group of leaders challenged Moses and Aaron, and how God answered.
16.p: Lord, You choose whom You will. Keep us humble, and teach us to honor those who serve You. Amen.
16.l: When you disagree with a leader today, say it respectfully and honestly instead of grumbling behind their back.
q: Moses gave the men a night to sleep on it. What decision do you need to sleep on before you act?

17.o: Enough had been done in the chapter before to quash all pretensions of the families of the tribe of Levi that would set up in competition with Aaron, and to make it appear that Aaron was the head of the tribe; but it seems, when that matter was settled, the princes of the rest of the tribes began to murmur. If the head of a tribe must be a priest, why not the head of some other tribe than that of Levi?
17.i: God settles a dispute over who should serve as priest by making Aaron's staff bud and bear almonds overnight.
17.p: Lord, You bring life from death. Make us fruitful in what You have called us to do. Amen.
17.l: Look at a seed or a bare branch today, and think about how God brings life from what looks dead.
q: God showed He had chosen Aaron by making a dry stick bloom. How do you see God bring life from dry places?

18.o: Aaron being now fully established in the priesthood abundantly to his own satisfaction, and to the satisfaction of the people (which was the good that God brought out of the evil opposition made to him), in this chapter God gives him full instructions concerning his office or rather repeats those which he had before given him. He tells him, I. What must be his work and the care and charge committed to him, and what assistance he should have the Levites in that work, ver. 1-7. II.
18.s: The Priests' Portion and Water for Cleansing
18.i: Numbers 18 and 19 explain who is responsible for the tent, how the priests and Levites were supported, and how someone who had touched death could come back.
18.p: Lord, thank You for making a way back for all who are far from You. Make us people who serve gladly and trust You for our portion. Amen.
18.l: Thank someone today who serves in your church or school, and tell them one thing you notice about their work.
q: The priests were paid for the office, not for their merit. Where have you treated a gift as if you had earned it?

19.o: This chapter is only concerning the preparing and using of the ashes which were to impregnate the water of purification. The people had complained of the strictness of the law, which forbade their near approach to the tabernacle, ch. xvii. 13. In answer to this complaint, they are here directed to purify themselves, so as that they might come as far as they had occasion without fear. Here is, I. The method of preparing these ashes, by the burning of a red heifer, with a great deal of ceremony, ver. 1-10. II.
19.s: The Priests' Portion and Water for Cleansing
19.i: Numbers 18 and 19 explain who is responsible for the tent, how the priests and Levites were supported, and how someone who had touched death could come back.
19.p: Lord, thank You for making a way back for all who are far from You. Make us people who serve gladly and trust You for our portion. Amen.
19.l: Thank someone today who serves in your church or school, and tell them one thing you notice about their work.
q: The priests were paid for the office, not for their merit. Where have you treated a gift as if you had earned it?

20.o: At this chapter begins the history of the fortieth year (which was the last year) of the Israelites' wandering in the wilderness. And since the beginning of their second year, when they were sentenced to perform their quarantine in the desert, there to wear away the tedious revolution of forty years, there is little recorded concerning them till this last year, which brought them to the borders of Canaan, and the history of this year is almost as large as the history of the first year.
20.i: Israel has no water at Kadesh, and Moses strikes the rock in anger, and God says he will not enter the land.
20.p: Lord, You are holy. Keep us from acting in anger, and help us to trust Your word. Amen.
20.l: When you are angry today, stop and take a breath before you speak or act.
q: God asked Moses to speak and Moses struck. When do you do something your way and not God's way?

21.o: The armies of Israel now begin to emerge out of the wilderness, and to come into a land inhabited, to enter upon action, and take possession of the frontiers of the land of promise. A glorious campaign this chapter gives us the history of, especially in the latter part of it. Here is, I. The defeat of Arad the Canaanite, ver. 1-3. II. The chastisement of the people with fiery serpents for their murmurings, and the relief granted them upon their submission by a brazen serpent, ver. 4-9. III.
21.i: Israel complains, snakes bite the people, and God heals those who look at a bronze snake on a pole.
21.p: Lord, we look to You. Heal us from the poison of our sin, and lift our eyes to Jesus. Amen.
21.l: When you are scared or hurting today, look up and ask God to help you.
q: Healing came by looking up in faith. Where do you need to look up and stop looking at the problem?

22.o: At this chapter begins the famous story of Balak and Balaam, their attempt to curse Israel, and the baffling of that attempt; God's people are long afterwards told to remember what Balak the king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, that they might know the righteousness of the Lord, Mic. vi. 5. In this chapter we have, I. Balak's fear of Israel, and the plot he had to get them cursed, ver. 1-4. II.
22.i: Balaam's donkey sees the angel that Balaam cannot, and God opens her mouth to speak.
22.p: Lord, open our eyes to see what You are doing, and keep us from running after reward. Amen.
22.l: Be kind to an animal today, and thank God for the way animals help us.
q: The donkey saw what the prophet could not. What are you missing that someone else can see?

23.o: In this chapter we have Balak and Balaam busy at work to do Israel a mischief, and, for ought that appears, neither Moses nor the elders of Israel know any thing of the matter, nor are in a capacity to break the snare; but God, who keeps Israel, and neither slumbers nor sleeps, baffles the attempt, without any intercession or contrivance of theirs. Here is, I. The first attempt to curse Israel. 1. The preparation made for it by sacrifice, ver. 1-3. 2. The contrary instruction God gave Balaam, ver. 4, 5. 3.
23.i: Numbers 23 and 24 tell how a king hired a seer to curse Israel, and how three tries ended in three blessings.
23.p: Lord, You protect Your people without their knowing. Thank You for turning curses into blessings. Amen.
23.l: Thank God today for protecting you from things you never knew about.
q: Balak thought he could bribe God with sacrifices. What do you give to God hoping he will give you what you want?

24.o: This chapter continues and concludes the history of the defeat of the counsels of Balak and Balaam against Israel, not by might, nor by power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts; and as great an instance it is of God's power over the children of men, and his favour towards his own children, as any of the victories recorded in the book of the wars of the Lord. What preparation was made the third time for the cursing of Israel we read of in the close of the foregoing chapter. In this chapter we are told, I.
24.i: Numbers 23 and 24 tell how a king hired a seer to curse Israel, and how three tries ended in three blessings.
24.p: Lord, You protect Your people without their knowing. Thank You for turning curses into blessings. Amen.
24.l: Thank God today for protecting you from things you never knew about.
q: Balak thought he could bribe God with sacrifices. What do you give to God hoping he will give you what you want?

25.o: Israel, having escaped the curse of Balaam, here sustains a great deal of damage and reproach by the counsel of Balaam, who, it seems, before he left Balak, put him into a more effectual way than that which Balak thought of to separate between the Israelites and their God. "The Lord will not be prevailed with by Balaam's charms to ruin them; try if they will not be prevailed with by the charms of the daughters of Moab to ruin themselves."
25.i: Numbers 25 is a dark chapter of idolatry and immorality at the edge of the promised land, and of the priest who stopped a plague.
25.p: Lord, keep us from idols of every kind. Give us zeal for Your honor and a love that does not hurt others. Amen.
25.l: Ask a grown-up to talk with you about why it is dangerous to follow what everyone else is doing.
q: If magistrates don't punish sin, God will. Where do you look away from wrong that is done openly?

26.o: This book is called Numbers, from the numberings of the children of Israel, of which it gives an account. Once they were numbered at Mount Sinai, in the first year after they came out of Egypt, which we had an account of, ch. i. and ii.. And now a second time they were numbered in the plains of Moab, just before they entered Canaan, and of this we have an account in this chapter. We have, I. Orders given for the doing of it, ver. 1-4. II. A register of the families and numbers of each tribe (ver.
26.i: Numbers 26 is a second head count, forty years on, and it shows exactly who stood at the edge of the promised land.
26.p: Lord, You keep Your promises across generations. Thank You for those who have walked with You a long time. Amen.
26.l: Notice someone older than you today, and ask them to tell you a story from when they were young.
q: The smallest tribe became one of the largest in forty years. Who or what looks too small to matter, and might not stay that way?

27.o: Here is, I. The case of Zelophehad's daughters determined, ver. 1-11. II. Notice given to Moses of his death approaching, ver. 12-14. III. Provision made of a successor in the government, 1. By the prayer of Moses, ver. 15-17. 2. By the appointment of God, ver. 18, &c.
27.i: Moses asks God for a shepherd for Israel, and God names Joshua, who is commissioned in front of the people.
27.p: Lord, give Your people faithful shepherds. Bless those who lead, and help us to follow. Amen.
27.l: Pray for a leader today, like a teacher, a pastor, or a parent, and ask God to give them wisdom.
q: Moses prayed for the people before he thought of himself. Who needs your prayers right now?

28.o: Now that the people were numbered, orders given for the dividing of the land, and a general of the forces nominated and commissioned, one would have expected that the next chapter should begin the history of the campaign, or at least should give us an account of the ordinances of war; no, it contains the ordinances of worship, and provides that now, as they were on the point of entering Canaan, they should be sure to take their religion along with them, and not forget this, in the prosecution of their wars, ver.
28.s: Every Day, Every Feast, Every Promise
28.i: Numbers 28 to 30 are the calendar of offerings for the whole year, followed by rules about keeping one's word.
28.p: Lord, You are worthy of our days, our mornings and evenings. Teach us to keep our word and to give with glad hearts. Amen.
28.l: Set a regular time today to say thank you to God, morning and evening, for a week.
q: The burnt offering meant giving oneself to God, soul and body. What small thing could you offer today as a daily habit?

29.o: This chapter appoints the offerings that were to be made by fire unto the Lord in the three great solemnities of the seventh month. I. In the feast of trumpets on the first day of that month, ver. 1-6. II. In the day of atonement on the tenth day, ver. 7-11. III. In the feast of tabernacles on the fifteenth day and the seven days following, ver. 12-38. And then the conclusion of these ordinances, ver. 39, 40.
29.s: Every Day, Every Feast, Every Promise
29.i: Numbers 28 to 30 are the calendar of offerings for the whole year, followed by rules about keeping one's word.
29.p: Lord, You are worthy of our days, our mornings and evenings. Teach us to keep our word and to give with glad hearts. Amen.
29.l: Set a regular time today to say thank you to God, morning and evening, for a week.
q: The burnt offering meant giving oneself to God, soul and body. What small thing could you offer today as a daily habit?

30.o: In this chapter we have a law concerning vows, which had been mentioned in the close of the foregoing chapter. I. Here is a general rule laid down that all vows must be carefully performed, ver. 1, 2. II. Some particular exceptions to this rule. 1. That the vows of daughters should not be binding unless allowed by the father, ver. 3-5. Nor, 2. The vows of wives unless allowed by the husband, ver. 6, &c.
30.s: Every Day, Every Feast, Every Promise
30.i: Numbers 28 to 30 are the calendar of offerings for the whole year, followed by rules about keeping one's word.
30.p: Lord, You are worthy of our days, our mornings and evenings. Teach us to keep our word and to give with glad hearts. Amen.
30.l: Set a regular time today to say thank you to God, morning and evening, for a week.
q: The burnt offering meant giving oneself to God, soul and body. What small thing could you offer today as a daily habit?

31.o: This chapter belongs to "the book of the wars of the Lord," in which it is probable it was inserted. It is the history of a holy war, a war with Midian. Here is, I. A divine command for the war, ver. 1, 2. II. The undertaking of the war, ver. 3-6. III. The glorious success of it, ver. 7-12. IV. Their triumphant return from the war. 1. The respect Moses paid to the soldiers, ver. 13. 2. The rebuke he gave them for sparing the women, ver. 14-18. 3.
31.i: Numbers 31 is the last battle Moses commanded, and one of the Bible's hardest chapters.
31.p: Lord, You are just and merciful. Help us to read hard chapters with honesty, and to trust You where we cannot understand. Amen.
31.l: Thank God today for protecting you and your family, and for the people who help keep you safe.
q: Whose quiet support makes your work possible?

32.o: In this chapter we have, I. The humble request of the tribes of Reuben and Gad for an inheritance on that side Jordan where Israel now lay encamped, ver. 1-5. II. Moses's misinterpretation of their request, ver. 6-15. III. Their explication of it, and stating it aright, ver. 16-19. IV. The grant of their petition under the provisos and limitations which they themselves proposed, ver. 20, &c.
32.i: Numbers 32 is a negotiation: two tribes ask to settle early, and Moses holds them to a promise.
32.p: Lord, keep us faithful to our promises, and teach us to care for our brothers and sisters before our own comfort. Amen.
32.l: Keep a promise today that you made to a friend or a family member, even if it takes extra effort.
q: Which one tempts you more when you choose a place to settle?

33.o: In this chapter we have, I. A particular account of the removals and encampments of the children of Israel, from their escape out of Egypt to their entrance into Canaan, forty-two in all, with some remarkable events that happened at some of those places, ver. 1-49. II. A strict command given them to drive out all the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, which they were not going to conquer and take possession of, ver. 50-56.
33.i: Numbers 33 is the travel diary of the exodus, written by Moses at God's command.
33.p: Lord, You went with Your people to every camp. Help us to remember Your faithfulness in every step. Amen.
33.l: Write down three places you have been this year, and thank God for something that happened at each.
q: God's way is not always the nearest way. Where are you being led around the long way right now, and what might you write in your journal about it?

34.o: In this chapter God directs Moses, and he is to direct Israel, I. Concerning the bounds and borders of the land of Canaan, ver. 1-15. II. Concerning the division and distribution of it to the tribes of Israel, ver. 16, &c.
34.s: Borders and a Promise About Inheritance
34.i: Numbers 34 and 36 mark out the borders of the promised land and make sure that no family's inheritance is lost.
34.p: Lord, You give each family a place. Thank You for fairness, and make us people who protect the inheritance of others. Amen.
34.l: Look at a map of where you live today, and thank God for a place to call home.
q: The border was a reminder of Egypt. What landmark near you reminds you of where you came from?

35.o: Orders having been given before for the dividing of the land of Canaan among the lay-tribes (as I may call them), care is here taken for a competent provision for the clergy, the tribe of Levi, which ministered in holy things. I. Forty-eight cities were to be assigned them, with their suburbs, some in every tribe, ver. 1-8. II. Six cities out of these were to be for cities of refuge, for any man that killed another unawares, ver. 9-15. In the law concerning these observe, 1.
35.i: God set up six cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, where someone who killed by accident could run for safety until he had a fair hearing.
35.p: Lord, You are our refuge. When we fail and are afraid, bring us running to You. Amen.
35.l: If you have made a mistake you are afraid to talk about, tell a grown-up you trust and let them help.
q: The refuge city gave safety and a fair hearing. Where do you need to run to God instead of hiding?

36.o: We have in this chapter the determination of another question that arose upon the case of the daughters of Zelophehad. God had appointed that they should inherit, ch. xxvii. 7. Now here, I. An inconvenience is suggested, in case they should marry into any other tribe, ver. 1-4. II.
